title: Delivered vs. promised
intro: Two lists, kept separate. On the left, what the administration can state without being knocked down: actions that are final, in force or signed into law, each confirmed in a primary federal source. On the right, the grassroots MAHA Promises Scorecard by former Kennedy campaign staff, tagged by the agency responsible. The lists mostly do not overlap: the scorecard covers pesticides, environment, farms and appointments; most solid wins are food, nutrition, drug prices and vaccines at HHS and USDA.
standard: A 'solid' win is final (signed law, final rule or order, adopted federal recommendation, or awarded funding) and verifiable at a .gov source. Voluntary pledges, proposed rules and reports are listed separately as 'real but limited'. Administration-reported figures are labeled as such.

items.say: The most significant reset of federal nutrition policy in decades: protein at every meal, full-fat dairy allowed, sharp limits on highly processed foods, added sugars and artificial additives. It is the basis for federal nutrition programs, including WIC and school meals.
items.careful: Guidance, not a ban. School-meal standards are still being rewritten to match it.

items.win: Whole Milk for Healthy Kids Act signed into law
items.say: Whole and 2% milk are back in school lunch and child nutrition programs. Bipartisan law (Marshall–Welch); USDA final rule issued May 8, 2026.
items.careful: Bipartisan bill; credit is shared with Congress.

items.win: SNAP soda and candy restrictions approved for 19 states
items.say: The first waivers ever to take soda and candy out of SNAP. 23 approved; 19 stand. In effect now in 8 states (AR, FL, ID, IN, LA, OK, TX, UT); 11 more start between Nov 2026 and 2028.
items.careful: A federal court vacated four approvals on Jun 22, 2026 (CO, IA, TN, WV). Say “19 states,” not 23.

items.win: Five natural food colors approved or expanded
items.say: Galdieria extract blue, butterfly pea flower (expanded), calcium phosphate (May 9, 2025), gardenia blue (Jul 14, 2025) and beetroot red: replacements that let companies drop petroleum dyes.
items.careful: Approving alternatives is not removing dyes; six petroleum dyes remain legal pending voluntary phase-out by end-2027.

items.win: Orange B revoked; Citrus Red No. 2 proposed for revocation
items.say: A final order removed Orange B from the food supply effective Sep 8, 2026.
items.careful: Orange B had not been certified for food since 1978, and Citrus Red No. 2 since 2020. Red No. 3's ban was issued Jan 15, 2025, under the prior administration. Do not claim it.

items.say: 26 drugmakers covering about 89% of the branded market signed MFN deals; TrumpRx.gov launched Feb 5, 2026; MFN prices extended to every state Medicaid program (Sep 2026). GLP-1s from $149 a month; $50 for eligible Medicare seniors.
items.careful: “$700M saved” and the price-decline claims are administration-reported figures. Cite them as such.

items.win: $50B Rural Health Transformation Program, awards to all 50 states
items.say: First-year awards of $147M–$281M per state, $10B a year through 2030, created by the Working Families Tax Cuts law. Georgia: $219M; Michigan: $173M; Wisconsin: $204M.
items.careful: Created by statute; CMS administers it.

items.win: Boxed warnings removed from menopause hormone therapy
items.say: Breast cancer, cardiovascular and dementia statements removed from the boxed warning on HRT; first six product labels approved Feb 12, 2026 (initiated Nov 10, 2025).
items.careful: The risks remain in the Warnings section; the endometrial-cancer boxed warning stays for estrogen-alone products.

items.win: Thimerosal (mercury) removed from all U.S. flu vaccines
items.say: Single-dose, thimerosal-free flu vaccines are now official CDC policy for children, pregnant women and all adults.
items.careful: Contested by medical groups; strong with the base.

items.win: Hospital pay no longer tied to staff COVID-vaccination reporting
items.say: The FY2026 inpatient payment final rule removed the COVID-19 vaccination coverage among health-care personnel measure from hospital quality reporting.
items.careful: Removes a reporting measure, not a mandate (the staff mandate ended in 2023).

tiers.label: Real, but voluntary, proposed or limited

items.win: Industry pledges to drop petroleum dyes
items.say: 27 of the largest food companies pledged to remove synthetic dyes; FDA targets the six remaining dyes for end-2027.
items.careful: Voluntary, no enforcement; the scorecard rates it partly kept.

items.win: GRAS self-certification rule proposed; first ultra-processed-food definition at final review
items.say: Companies would have to notify FDA before using a self-affirmed “GRAS” ingredient.
items.careful: Proposed, not final. Finalizing it is the single cleanest available win.

items.win: 76 medical schools in 36 states commit to 40 hours of nutrition education
items.say: Starting fall 2026, plus eight accrediting and board organizations.
First full review of formula nutrient requirements since 1998; more heavy-metal testing.
items.careful: Administrative review; no new enforceable standard yet.

items.say: Final rule listed for Dec 2026 on FDA's agenda.
items.careful: Proposed under the prior administration; not final.

items.win: CDC told to stop recommending community water fluoridation
items.say: Federal recommendation withdrawn; Utah and Florida banned added fluoride.
items.careful: Nonbinding and late, per the scorecard (partly kept). The state bans are state actions.

tiers.label: Done, but contested or in court

items.win: Childhood schedule realigned: 11 diseases recommended for all children, down from 18
items.say: CDC decision memo (Jan 5, 2026) and executive orders (May 29 and Aug 2026) move hepatitis A/B, rotavirus, meningococcal, flu and COVID to shared decision-making; COVID shots dropped for healthy children and pregnant women (May 2025).
items.careful: The August order itself says implementation was delayed by litigation over ACIP's composition. Public trust in the childhood schedule fell from 71% to 62% (Axios-Ipsos). Strong with the base, risky with swing voters.

scorecard.name: MAHA Promises Scorecard
scorecard.author: Tiffany Cianci, with former Kennedy campaign staff (released Oct 8, 2026)
scorecard.method: Kept = concrete, enforceable action; voluntary agreements do not count. Partially kept = incomplete, nonbinding, contradicted or late. Broken = contrary action, program eliminated, or no action.
scorecard.agency_note: Agency tags are the tracker's, assigned from each item's description; the scorecard does not tag items by agency.
items: 68% of EPA/DOE/DOI nominees tied to regulated industries
Chemical-industry insider in top EPA post
Paraquat announcement with no new action
Amicus brief for Bayer at the Supreme Court
Organic program staff cut by a third

takeaways: 35 of the scorecard's 37 “broken” items are EPA, USDA, White House or DOJ actions. Of its 5 HHS items, 3 are rated partly kept.

The two lists barely overlap. The scorecard tracks pesticides, environment, farms and appointments. Most solid wins (Dietary Guidelines, whole milk, SNAP waivers, drug prices, HRT labels) are not on it.
The defensible message is “HHS is delivering on food, prices and choice; the fights still open are at EPA and USDA,” not “every promise kept.”
Pesticides are the gap with no offsetting win: 7 of 7 broken, and the movement's sharpest grievance (glyphosate).
